docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents the hub subsystem of RadioLink, Team 105's embedded project. It is written so the design can be reviewed on its own, without the team report open beside it.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: RadioLink is a hub-and-spoke system, and this board is the hub. It has an on-board OLED for graphics, a debug LED, and three UART ports. Board 1 carries the microphone, board 2 carries the pushbuttons and a temperature sensor, and board 3 carries the speaker. The microphone and button boards send their data to the hub. The hub shows a custom interface on the OLED, which is navigated with board 2's buttons, and it plays the microphone signal through the speaker.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
My work on RadioLink has centered on concept ideation, user-needs benchmarking, and the hub itself. The hub receives the microphone and temperature data, presents it on a custom OLED interface that is navigated with the pushbuttons, and sends the microphone signal to the speaker.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram is the hub subsystem of RadioLink, Team 105's hub-and-spoke design. A Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano sits at the center. A computer supplies 5 V over USB. An LM7805 provides a regulated 5 V rail rated for 1 A, and a separate 3.3 V regulator rated for 500 mA powers the display.

The microcontroller drives a 128x64 SSD1306 OLED (ER-OLED0.96-1.3W) over I2C. SDA is RB2 and SCL is RB1. The OLED side of that bus is 3.3 V, and the microcontroller side is 5 V. A red LED is driven from RA2 using PWM.

Three UART ports connect this hub to the other boards. Each link is 5 V and uses an RX/TX pair:

  • Connector 1: RX on RC3, TX on RC2
  • Connector 2: RX on RF1, TX on RF0
  • Connector 3: RX on RA4, TX on RA3

These ports connect to the microphone board, the button and temperature board, and the speaker board. The microphone and button boards send data in. The hub shows temperature readings and the audio path on the OLED, and it sends the microphone signal out to the speaker.

Rationale: Option 1 is widely used, well documented, and readily available. Its 1.5 A output also provides plenty of current for the circuit. The through-hole package makes it easy to prototype.

docs.title: How the Choices Meet the Requirements
docs.text:
The hub has to show a custom screen and exchange UART data with the microphone, button, and speaker boards. The display needs to be small, readable, and driven by a bus the PIC18F57Q43 already has. Option 3 was selected because it uses the SSD1306, costs $2.49, and can be ordered without the 12- and 16-week waits of the larger panels. A 0.96-inch screen is enough for the temperature reading and the audio status that the user pages through with the buttons on board 2.

The 9 V barrel jack has to become 5 V for the Curiosity Nano, the debug LED, and the UART logic. The L7805 does that and is easy to solder. The power budget shows the hub itself uses under 100 mA, so the deciding factors were the 9 V input and the through-hole package, not a need for the full 1.5 A. The MCP1702 is the better low-power part, and it was set aside because 250 mA and a SOT-23 package are not what this build needs.

docs.title: MCC Configuration
docs.text:
The hub uses the PIC18F57Q43 on the Curiosity Nano. The clock is the internal HFINTOSC. There is no external crystal on the schematic. Peripheral pin select maps the digital pins below.

Function Peripheral Pins System clock HFINTOSC Internal OLED I2C SDA on RB2, SCL on RB1 Debug LED PWM RA2 UART connector 1 UART TX on RC2, RX on RC3 UART connector 2 UART TX on RF0, RX on RF1 UART connector 3 UART TX on RA3, RX on RA4 Debug button GPIO input SW1. The schematic does not label which PIC pin it uses.

The three UART ports are the links to the microphone board, the button and temperature board, and the speaker board. The block diagram does not assign a connector number to a specific board, so this table does not either. I2C is shifted from 5 V at the microcontroller to 3.3 V at the OLED. SW1 is the debug button on this board, not the user buttons on board 2.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is the hub subsystem of RadioLink for Team 105. It is centered on a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano. The hub reads the microphone board and the button and temperature board over UART, shows that information on a 128x64 SSD1306 OLED, sends the microphone signal to the speaker board, and drives a local debug LED.

Power comes from a 9 V barrel jack. A 1 A fuse feeds an LM7805, which regulates that input to 5 V for the microcontroller and the UART connectors. A separate 3.3 V supply powers the OLED. BSS138 level shifters translate the I2C signals between the 5 V microcontroller and the 3.3 V display. Test points, a pushbutton, and the red LED provide debugging access on the microcontroller side. Three 8-pin connectors carry the UART links to the other subsystems.

Figure 1: Hub subsystem schematic for RadioLink, showing the microcontroller and debug circuitry, the OLED and I2C interface, 9 V input and 5 V regulation, and the three UART connectors.

docs.title: Function
docs.text:
RadioLink needs one board that can take the microphone and the button and temperature data, show it, and pass the microphone audio to the speaker. This schematic is that board.

The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is the controller. Three UART connectors are the links to the other boards. One brings in the microphone, one brings in the pushbuttons and the temperature reading, and one carries the microphone signal out to the speaker. The connectors are logic-level RX and TX. They do not feed power to those boards, so the speaker amplifier is not a load on this schematic.

The 128x64 OLED is the interface the user sees. Board 2's buttons move through that screen. The display is a 3.3 V part, and the microcontroller I2C pins are 5 V, so Q1 and Q2 (BSS138) level-shift SDA and SCL. JP1 opens the display supply so the OLED can be powered down without shutting off the hub.

The 9 V barrel jack, the 1 A fuse, and the LM7805 make the 5 V rail for the microcontroller, the debug LED, and the UART logic. U2 makes the 3.3 V rail for the OLED. The red LED and SW1 are debug parts on this board. They are not the user controls. Those controls stay on board 2.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This budget is for the RadioLink hub only. It covers the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, the on-board OLED, the debug LED, and the regulators that feed them. The microphone, button, and speaker boards are not included. Their UART links are logic-level signals, and those boards carry their own supplies.

Currents are datasheet or circuit limits, not lab measurements. The template's 25% margin is kept on each rail. The spreadsheet is linked below.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
After the 25% margin, the hub asks the 5 V rail for 72.5 mA. The 1 A fuse and the LM7805 can both supply that, with 927.5 mA still unused. The OLED is the largest load, at 33 mA on the 3.3 V rail. The 3.3 V regulator is rated for 500 mA on the block diagram, so the display does not stress it.

The LM7805 drops 9 V to 5 V. At this load its dissipation is about 0.36 W, which a TO-220 package can handle without a heatsink. The 9 V input, limited by the 1 A fuse, still has 919.5 mA of spare current. That spare current is not a reason to power the speaker from this board. The speaker amplifier belongs on board 3.

A 500 mAh 9 V alkaline battery would run this hub for 6.21 hours. The schematic uses a barrel jack, so that figure only applies if a battery is substituted for the jack. USB on the Curiosity Nano can power the microcontroller during programming, and that path is separate from this 9 V budget.
